analysis.one_liner: Limits interest deductions that inverted corporations use to shift U.S. profits offshore.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 15 Senate Democrats, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a U.S. company moves its headquarters overseas on paper to lower its taxes but keeps its operations in America, the new foreign parent often loads the U.S. company with debt and the U.S. side pays large, tax-deductible interest payments to its own parent abroad. This bill would cap those interest deductions at 25% of taxable income for such companies, block carrying unused deductions forward, and require them to get IRS sign-off on deals with their foreign affiliates for ten years. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. taxpayers generally, who would collect more revenue from multinationals that reduce their American tax bills by paper inversion and related-party interest payments, and domestic competitors who currently face a tax disadvantage against inverted rivals.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the interest deduction for U.S. members of inverted corporate groups at 25% of adjusted taxable income and eliminates the carryforward of disallowed interest, directly targeting the 'earnings stripping' technique [S2][S3].

Requires these companies to file annual applications for IRS approval agreements on related-party transactions for ten years, with heavy penalties (losing deductions and disregarding intangible transfers) if they fail to comply [S2][S3].

Expands the definition of an inverted ('surrogate foreign') corporation to catch groups that are majority foreign-owned, including deals completed before or after enactment, closing loopholes in the existing inversion rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that have inverted or would invert: they would pay more U.S. tax by losing interest deductions and facing stricter scrutiny of transactions with their foreign affiliates.

drawbacks.text: A steeper limit on interest deductions for inverted groups only could push some investment and headquarters decisions further abroad, since the penalty applies only to companies that invert rather than fixing the underlying incentive to locate profits outside the United States (an argument critics of targeted anti-inversion rules commonly make; the bill text and sources do not include economic estimates) [S3].

The requirement for annual IRS approval agreements on related-party transactions would add significant compliance paperwork and administrative burden for affected companies for ten years after inversion [S2][S3].

The bill addresses only one tax-avoidance technique used by inverted firms; it would not raise the corporate revenue that a broader international tax overhaul would, and companies not covered by the inverted-corporation definition could still shift profits through other channels [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, targeted fix: it protects tax revenue from a specific avoidance technique without touching the broader corporate tax code. Its main weakness is that it taxes a symptom rather than the disease — companies not meeting the inversion definition can still strip earnings, and targeted penalties can nudge more companies toward full inversion. On balance, for ordinary taxpayers the revenue protection outweighs the added compliance burden on a small set of corporations, but it is a partial remedy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there until the two-year Congress ended, with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action.

narrative.text: Senator Charles Schumer introduced the bill on September 10, 2014, with 14 Democratic cosponsors including Senators Durbin, Brown, Warren, and Levin [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last recorded action on the bill [S5].

The Finance Committee took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, killing the bill under the rule that legislation does not carry over to the next Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that use inversions and earnings stripping kept the ability to deduct interest paid to their own foreign parents, saving them U.S. tax at the cost of revenue the bill would have preserved for other taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Inverted corporations and their foreign parents

for.name: Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill targeting earnings stripping by inverted corporations.

for.name: 14 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Senators Durbin, Brown, Coons, Rockefeller, Stabenow, Cardin, Reed, Menendez, Markey, Merkley, Baldwin, Levin, and Warren.

for.name: U.S. Treasury Department
for.what_they_did: Announced its own anti-inversion regulatory actions in the same period, reflecting parallel executive attention to the practice.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 10, 2014 and took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and the bill never advanced in the Senate.

industries.industry: Inverted multinational corporations and their U.S. subsidiaries
industries.note: These companies would lose interest deductions above 25% of taxable income and face IRS approval requirements on related-party deals, directly reducing a major tax-saving strategy. Their savings come at the expense of U.S. tax revenue [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Tax advisory and accounting firms serving multinationals
industries.note: Stricter deduction limits and mandatory IRS approval agreements would reduce demand for structuring cross-border interest and transfer-pricing arrangements [S3].

industries.industry: Domestic U.S. corporations that remain headquartered in the United States
industries.note: Competitors that exploit inversion and interest deductions gain a tax advantage; the bill would narrow that gap, and the revenue preserved reduces pressure on other taxpayers [S3].
